title: Support reading password-protected xlsx
description:
Closes #794

There's been a recurring wish for readxl to be able to read password protected files. I was reluctant to add that feature if it brought in onerous dependencies, e.g. Java. But I recently did another search for feasibility and that surfaced <https://github.com/JanMarvin/msoc>, an R package from the author of [openxlsx2](https://github.com/JanMarvin/openxlsx2). (It's explicit that msoc will never be released to CRAN BTW.) The msoc package inspired me to take a look at <https://github.com/herumi/msoffice> and lead to this PR. This is a ground-up effort to vendor just the decryption parts of `herumi/msoffice` into readxl.

## Overview

An encrypted xlsx is an OLE2 compound file, with the same magic bytes as a legacy xls, that holds `EncryptionInfo` and `EncryptedPackage` streams. Decrypting the latter yields the ordinary xlsx zip. So the new feature is: recognize such a file, decrypt it to a tempfile, and hand the tempfile to the existing xlsx reader. Nothing downstream of the file path changes.

The decryption code is the decrypt-only subset of [herumi/msoffice](https://github.com/herumi/msoffice)'s C++ headers (BSD-3), including the cybozu crypto headers it bundles, vendored into `src/msoffice/`. [msoc](https://github.com/JanMarvin/msoc), which wraps the same library, was the inspiration, but no code comes from it.

The new `password` argument appears only in `read_xlsx()` and `excel_sheets()`. Because you can't distinguish encrypted xlsx from xls based on magic bytes, I really wanted to incorporate the feature in functions that are explicitly targetting xlsx, like `read_xlsx()`. Sadly, I don't have an xlsx-only version of `excel_sheets()`, so I had to just cope there.

cli and rlang are new in `Imports` but were already hard indirect dependencies (via tibble) and I do want to incorporate them here more broadly anyway.

### Platform support

AES always comes from the CPU or the OS, never OpenSSL. Where neither provides it, decryption is compiled out: readxl still installs, and errors informatively on an encrypted file.

| Platform | AES backend | CI job |
|---|---|---|
| x86-64 (Linux, Windows, Intel macOS) | AES-NI | ubuntu-latest, windows-latest |
| Apple Silicon | CommonCrypto | macos-latest |
| Windows on ARM | bcrypt | windows-11-arm (new) |
| Linux on ARM, webR, and the rest | none, decryption compiled out | ubuntu-24.04-arm (new) |

### How to review

You probably want to look at the net diff, more than individual commits. (Up 'til 3251b57, I was letting an agent run with high-level supervision until we had an MVP. From 67088b7 onwards, I was heavily involved.)

Most of `src/msoffice/` can be skipped. It was imported byte-identical from msoffice b5fed29 in f263dd7 and then LF-normalized. Every readxl edit since then is fenced with `// --- Start readxl ---` / `// --- End readxl ---`, with the upstream code kept as a comment, and `git diff --ignore-cr-at-eol f263dd7 HEAD -- src/msoffice` shows just those changes. They fall into three groups:

- Build and CRAN hygiene: no `#pragma GCC diagnostic`, no cybozu File/Mmap (their headers collide with R's), no encryption-only RNG, and no OpenSSL include alongside CommonCrypto.
- Silencing diagnostics that upstream prints unconditionally for standard-encrypted files.
- Two bug fixes to length arithmetic in `decode.hpp`. These are the only changes to upstream's decryption logic.

Generated files, the binary fixtures, and `.posit/assistant/settings.json` (unrelated tooling) can also be skipped.

### Tricky bits and trade-offs

- **Keep format detection and decryption separate, as much as possible.** `read_xlsx()` peeks at the 8-byte signature and only probes for encryption if it sees OLE2, which a real xlsx never has. `excel_sheets()` also serves xls, where an OLE2 signature is normal, so it can't tell a real xls from an encrypted xlsx without the expensive probe. Instead it tries the normal route first, probes only on failure, and re-raises the original error if the file isn't encrypted.
- **Plaintext on disk.** A decrypted copy of the workbook sits in `tempdir()` for the duration of the call. `on.exit()` removes it, but a hard crash would leave it behind. Reading xlsx from memory would be far more work than this warrants. In the same spirit of pragmatism, an encrypted file is read into memory twice (probe, then decrypt).
- **Size and build time.** The shared library gets about a third bigger (0.38 → 0.50 MB on macOS; 3.8 → 5.2 MB on Linux, where builds embed debug symbols), and that accounts for essentially all of the change in installed size. Building takes about a second longer (6 s → 7 s for a macOS binary).

### CI

R CMD check passes on all 10 jobs with no WARNINGs, so there are no significant compiler warnings under default flags. The 13 decryption tests skip on ubuntu-24.04-arm, which is there to show that the compiled-out build installs and errors cleanly. I've done some r-hub runs along the way and here's the latest: https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/actions/runs/38607732434. (I am not worried about the failure to build vignettes when rmarkdown is not installed.)

title: Return blank cells for a fully specified range with no data
description:
Reading a fully specified `range` that contains no cells (a blank sheet, or a blank region of a non-empty sheet) returned a 0 x 0 tibble:

``` r
read_excel("blank.xlsx", range = "A1:C1", col_names = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 0 x 0
```

`insertShims()` returned early when no cells were loaded, so the corner shim cells that pad a `range` to its requested size were never added. This is the only case where a `range` was not honoured: it was already padded when the range overlapped any data.

Now, when all four limits of the range are specified and no cells were found, the two corner shims are added, giving a 1 x 3 tibble of `NA`s above. Open-ended ranges such as `cell_rows(1:3)` still return 0 x 0, since their extent is unknown, and `skip`/`n_max` are untouched.

I compared 75 calls (xlsx and xls; bounded, single-cell, R1C1, open-ended, `skip`/`n_max`, `col_names`, `col_types`, `na`) before and after: only the 36 calls that previously returned 0 x 0 for a fully bounded range changed.

Closes #550

title: Support reading password-protected xlsx (tiny-AES-c alternative to #802)
description:
Closes #794
Closes #802 (I'm happy to use this approach instead and have started working here now)

Changes by @jennybc:

* Use the compound file reading capabilities that we already have in libxls vs. rolling our own (7e50e3ce6eed95955ba704596714e0f2d3b30700).
* Refactor on the R side to check format earlier. Now that we've taken more control, we can actually make a cheap format check (is this xls? xlsx? encrypted xlsx?) and do things in a more logical way (e65b2429c6219860f39429ac4c6e10083ed7b20f).
* Work on error handling. My local agent did lots of fuzz testing and manual tests with truncated files and that suggested a few fixes.

---

*Original description*

This is an alternative to #802. It keeps the same R interface, tests, and fixtures, but swaps the vendored msoffice/cybozu code (~8k lines, platform-specific AES backends) for a much smaller, fully portable implementation.

## Background

An encrypted xlsx is an OLE2 compound file holding two streams. `EncryptionInfo` describes how to derive the key from the password (an iterated SHA-1/SHA-2 hash) and `EncryptedPackage` is the original xlsx zip, encrypted with AES. So decryption needs a small OLE2 reader, a few hash functions, and AES.

## Implementation

- **`src/tinyaes/`**: [tiny-AES-c](https://github.com/kokke/tiny-AES-c), vendored unmodified (public domain, commit 2385675). It fixes the key size at compile time, so `aes128.c`, `aes192.c`, and `aes256.c` each compile it under distinct symbol names via `src/aes-variant.h`.
- **`src/sha.h`**: minimal one-shot SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512. All four were checked against `openssl dgst` on inputs of various lengths, including the padding edge cases.
- **`src/Decrypt.cpp`**: a small OLE2 (CFB) reader plus ECMA-376 standard (AES-ECB) and agile (AES-CBC) decryption per [MS-OFFCRYPTO]. The agile XML is parsed with readxl's bundled rapidxml.
- **R side**: R reads the file bytes and passes them to C++, which avoids native path encoding issues. The password is converted to UTF-16LE with `iconv()`. The decrypted zip goes to a tempfile, as in #802.

## Differences from #802

- Plain portable C/C++ with no CommonCrypto, bcrypt, or AES-NI, so decryption works on all platforms, including Linux on ARM and webR. `decryption_available()`, `check_decryption_available()`, `skip_if_no_decryption()`, and the platform caveats in the docs and NEWS are removed.
- The "decryption unavailable on this platform" test and its snapshot were dropped, since that case no longer exists. All other tests are unchanged.
- No extra link flags (`-lbcrypt`) or `CYBOZU_*` defines.
- The ARM CI jobs from #802 are kept, and now actually run the decryption tests.

## Testing

- `devtools::test()`: 430 passing, 0 failures, 0 skips.
- The new sources compile without warnings under `-Wall -Wextra -pedantic`.
- About 1,200 randomly corrupted or truncated copies of the fixtures all fail cleanly (R error or "wrong password"), with no crashes.
- AES-192 and SHA-256/384 have no fixture files. Excel itself writes SHA-512 with AES-256.

title: Allow `format-suggest` to check out fork PR heads under `pull_request_target`
description:
The `format-suggest` GitHub Actions job was failing before formatting ran because `actions/checkout@v4` now blocks fork PR checkout in `pull_request_target` workflows unless it is explicitly allowed. This updates the workflow to opt into that checkout path while narrowing credential exposure.

- **Workflow checkout**
  - opt into fork-head checkout for the formatting job
  - disable persisted git credentials for the checkout step

- **Resulting workflow change**
  ```yaml
  - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    with:
      ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      persist-credentials: false
      allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true
  ```

title: Reject NA sheet and integer-overflow limits in read_excel()
description:
### sheet = NA crashes with an internal error

standardise_sheet() checked the sheet number with `if (sheet < 1)`. A numeric NA made the comparison NA and R failed before reaching the intended message:

```r
read_excel(path, sheet = NA_real_)
#> Error: missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
```

The positivity check now rejects NA first and keeps the same error.

### Large limits overflow to NA and drop the read cap

standardise_limits() maps NA to -1, the "unspecified" sentinel, and did so before converting to integer. A limit above .Machine$integer.max overflowed to NA inside as.integer() and passed through as unspecified, so the cap disappeared. A 150-row sheet read with n_max = 1e10 returned all 150 rows:

```r
read_excel(path, n_max = 1e10)
#> Warning: NAs introduced by coercion to integer range
#> # A tibble: 150 x 5
```

The conversion now runs first, entries that were NA only after the conversion trigger an error naming the offending limit, and only originally-NA entries become -1.
With n_max = 1e10 the error is "`max_row` limit is too large to be represented as an integer".

Found during my most recent [ry](https://github.com/sims1253/ry) audit.

title: Adopt a different convention re order of includes
description:
Fixes #775 and, hopefully, heads off future Alpine issues of this nature.

Exactly why I was ordering includes as I was has been lost in the sands of time. But this seems more conventional:

system → cpp11 → other vendored (libxls, rapidxml) → project

Within the group, alphabetical. Blank lines between.

For a .cpp file, the corresponding .h sits at the top.

Why system before libxls? we want standard headers like `<stdint.h>` processed in the global namespace, not inside xls. This is #775. (And pretty similar stories in #562, #676, #714.)

Why cpp11 before libxls? libxls transitively pulls in <Rinternals.h> via cran.h, and cpp11 needs to set R_NO_REMAP/STRICT_R_HEADERS before any R header is processed

title: Avoid cpp11::warning / cpp11::stop variadic forwarding
description:
Closes #784

readxl segfaults in various places:

- r-universe (segfault; reported in #784)
- CRAN: `r-devel-linux-x86_64-{debian,fedora}-clang` (segfault); `r-release-macos-x86_64` (segfault);
 https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_readxl.html.
- Local: macOS arm64, Apple clang 21, with the "right" compilation flags.

Whether you see a segfault or some other failure mode (e.g. indefinitie hang) appear to depend on compilation flags. Some of these other presentations are seen:

- CRAN's additional checks on `M1Mac` ("Warning: elapsed-time limit of 1.5 hours reached for sub-process")
- readxl's own CI on macos-latest, e.g. https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/actions/runs/25193092291/job/73867448241. I've had to just kill those jobs.
- Locally, with default compilation flags.

From bisection, it appears to be a regression triggered by upgrading cpp11 from 0.5.3 to 0.5.4 (released 2026-04-09 on CRAN).

Claude Code analysis: lldb shows the crash deep inside cpp11's `safe[Rf_warningcall]` machinery — specifically `std::tuple_leaf::get(this=0x0000ffff01000000)` while `apply()` is unpacking the tuple of forwarded references that the closure passed to `R_UnwindProtect` was built from. The leaf address is corrupted (the 0xffff... pattern looks PAC-failure-like, but the same crash hits Linux clang 21 with no PAC, so likely a generic codegen/lifetime issue rather than PAC).

Workaround taken in this PR: format warning and stop messages into a `std::string` ourselves and call `Rf_warningcall` / `Rf_errorcall` directly inside `cpp11::unwind_protect`. This keeps longjmp protection but avoids cpp11's variadic-template arg forwarding entirely.

Filed upstream at https://github.com/r-lib/cpp11/issues/491

title: Fix compilation on Alpine Linux
description:
and other systems that use musl.

The problem is that the internal musl header that defines
`uid_t` and `gid_t` only defines it conditionally, if a macro is set.
This macro is set if the header is included from `unistd.h`,
but not if included from another header.

readxl uses `#pragma once`, so the header will not be included
twice, so `uid_t` might not be defined, if unistd.h is not
included early on.

The same story happens with `struct timeval` and `sys/time.h`.

Closes https://github.com/r-hub/r-minimal/issues/40

title: Don't misinterpret colors as dates
description:
Fixes #388
Closes #692

This caught me again recently.

Excel number formats support colours for, e.g. negative values `0.00;0.00[Red]`. Currently the `d` in `Red` (and some letters of other colours) is confused with the `d` in a date format `dd/mm/yyyy`, so the cell is incorrectly treated as a `date` cell.

The tests force a warning if this happens, by explicitly setting `col_type = "numeric"`.

The 'lowercase' variant of the test spreadsheet uses `red` (and similar) rather than `Red`, because this is allowed by the spec, though Excel itself doesn't create such files.

title: Push re-encoding of xls path into XlsWorkBook constructor
description:
I'm making this PR to restore symmetry of `read_xls_()` and `read_xlsx_()`. I want their signature and body to be the same (for eventual de-deduplication). The symmetry was lost at the time of the Rcpp --> cpp11 conversion (33c79a58).

General recap of this path handling:

* User's path needs to be normalized to expand, e.g., a leading `~/`. At least for xls, we need to do this (see #498).
* As of R 3.5, `normalizePath()` (`path.expand()`, really) returns UTF-8 encoded output, even if the input was not UTF-8.
* Once we adopted cpp11, it also does automatic conversion to UTF-8 for strings.
* This is fine for xlsx because we ultimately open the file with R (see `zip_buffer()` in [`R/xlsx-zip.R`](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/d8f789e173b42cb213b8da14979c11aa300eb38e/R/xlsx-zip.R)).
* For xls, we need to re-encode to the native encoding before we pass the path to libxls, which [uses `fopen()`](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/d8f789e173b42cb213b8da14979c11aa300eb38e/src/libxls/ole.c#L625).

Relevant previous history:

* https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/pull/477
* https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/pull/499

``` r
library(readxl)
```

title: Prepare for changes re: name repair in tibble
description:
The new `.name_repair` looks good! Consider this a pilot test for what other downstream packages will need to do.

To support new tibble, I had to stop calling `as_tibble()` with the `validate` argument  and start passing `.name_repair`, with a readxl default value of "unique".

Vast majority of my changes are around messaging.

---

``` r
devtools::load_all()
#> Loading readxl

utils::packageVersion("tibble")
#> [1] '1.4.99.9005'
```

Working with a test sheet in which all col names are the empty string.

readxl default behavior = `.name_repair = “unique”`

``` r
read_excel(
  test_sheet("no-yes-col-names.xlsx"),
  sheet = "empty-col-names"
)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> `..1`
#> * `` -> `..2`
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   ..1   ..2  
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a     b
```

Demonstrating all the promised flexibility of `.repair_names` is now available here! First, using levels “minimal” and “universal”.

``` r
read_excel(
  test_sheet("no-yes-col-names.xlsx"),
  sheet = "empty-col-names",
  .name_repair = "minimal"
)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   ``    ``   
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a     b

read_excel(
  test_sheet("no-yes-col-names.xlsx"),
  sheet = "empty-col-names",
  .name_repair = "universal"
)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ...1
#> * `` -> ...2
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   ...1  ...2 
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a     b
```

Now I pass a custom namer.

``` r
LETTER_names <- function(nms) LETTERS[seq_along(nms)]
read_excel(
  test_sheet("no-yes-col-names.xlsx"),
  sheet = "empty-col-names",
  .name_repair = LETTER_names
)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   A     B    
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a     b
```

Using a purrr-style formula to use `base::make.names()`

``` r
read_excel(
  test_sheet("no-yes-col-names.xlsx"),
  sheet = "empty-col-names",
  .name_repair = ~ make.names(., unique = TRUE)
)
#> # A tibble: 1 x 2
#>   X     X.1  
#>   <chr> <chr>
#> 1 a     b
```

I propose a functionality to filter excel sheets by using wild card or regular expression. For example:

```r
excel_sheets(readxl_example("datasets.xlsx"))

excel_sheets(readxl_example("datasets.xlsx"), glob = "??i*")
```

title: Adapt to tibble v1.4.99.* and ruminate on name repair
description:
For discussion. This PR

1. Adapts to the deprecation of `validate` in `as_tibble()`, i.e. it uses the new `.tidy_names` argument.
1. Intercepts `.tidy_names = TRUE` and `.tidy_names = some_function`, in order to capture the names before and after repair and return them in the `names_history` attribute of the returned tibble. This is in the same spirit as the "problems" reported by readr.

Reminder of what `.tidy_names` does:

https://github.com/tidyverse/tibble/blob/e816ba30ad227f7018a1868a66cc324d53589ffd/R/tibble.R#L26-L31

```
#' @param .tidy_names Treatment of invalid or duplicate column names:
#'   - `NULL`: default, throw an error if there are any missing or duplicated names,
#'   - `FALSE`: deliberately request a tibble with invalid names,
#'   - `TRUE`: apply [tidy_names()] to the names,
#'   - a function: apply custom name repair (e.g., `.tidy_names = make.names`
#'     to get base R equivalence).
```

This adds quite a lot of code and requires adding rlang to Imports (or copying code from tibble and rlang into readxl). There are some changes that could be made in tibble to make this easier (e.g. https://github.com/tidyverse/tibble/issues/462).

We could also decide to decline to report on name repair. If user wants such info, they should prevent name repair via `read_excel(..., .tidy_names = FALSE)` and do it themselves after the fact.

(I haven't fixed tests or NEWS yet ... but this does work, usage below.)

---

``` r
devtools::load_all(".")
#> Loading readxl

path <- test_sheet("unnamed-duplicated-columns.xlsx")

read_excel(path)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ..1
#> * var2 -> var2..2
#> * `` -> ..3
#> * var2 -> var2..4
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>     ..1 var2..2   ..3 var2..4
#>   <dbl> <chr>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1 a         1.1 aa     
#> 2     2 b         2.1 bb
read_excel(path, .tidy_names = TRUE) # the default
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ..1
#> * var2 -> var2..2
#> * `` -> ..3
#> * var2 -> var2..4
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>     ..1 var2..2   ..3 var2..4
#>   <dbl> <chr>   <dbl> <chr>  
#> 1     1 a         1.1 aa     
#> 2     2 b         2.1 bb

read_excel(path, .tidy_names = NULL)
#> Error: Columns 1, 3 must be named.

read_excel(path, .tidy_names = FALSE)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>      `` var2     `` var2 
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1 a       1.1 aa   
#> 2     2 b       2.1 bb

## base R name repair
read_excel(path, .tidy_names = make.names)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>       X var2      X var2 
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1 a       1.1 aa   
#> 2     2 b       2.1 bb

## emulating behaviour of readxl v1.1.0
f <- function(x) {
  x <- tibble::repair_names(x, prefix = "X", sep = "__")
  names(x)
}
read_excel(path, .tidy_names = f)
#> # A tibble: 2 x 4
#>    X__1 X__2   X__3 X__4 
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <chr>
#> 1     1 a       1.1 aa   
#> 2     2 b       2.1 bb


## now let's look at names before / after
x <- read_excel(path, .tidy_names = TRUE)
#> New names:
#> * `` -> ..1
#> * var2 -> var2..2
#> * `` -> ..3
#> * var2 -> var2..4
attr(x, "names_history")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   before after  
#>   <chr>  <chr>  
#> 1 ""     ..1    
#> 2 var2   var2..2
#> 3 ""     ..3    
#> 4 var2   var2..4

x <- read_excel(path, .tidy_names = make.names)
attr(x, "names_history")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   before after
#>   <chr>  <chr>
#> 1 ""     X    
#> 2 var2   var2 
#> 3 ""     X    
#> 4 var2   var2

x <- read_excel(path, .tidy_names = f)
attr(x, "names_history")
#> # A tibble: 4 x 2
#>   before after
#>   <chr>  <chr>
#> 1 ""     X__1 
#> 2 var2   X__2 
#> 3 ""     X__3 
#> 4 var2   X__4
```

title: libxls gcc5/6/7 fix
description:
Wasn't compiling because `ssize_t` was undefined.

```
gcc [...]   -fpic  -O2 -march=native -std=c99  -c endian.c -o endian.o
In file included from ./libxls/xlsstruct.h:40:0,
                 from libxls/endian.h:30,
                 from endian.c:33:
./libxls/ole.h:174:1: error: unknown type name ‘ssize_t’
 extern ssize_t ole2_read(void* buf,size_t size,size_t count,OLE2Stream* olest);
 ^
make: *** [endian.o] Error 1
ERROR: compilation failed for package ‘readxl’
```

`ssize_t` should be defined in `stdio.h`, according to [POSIX 2008](http://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/stdio.h.html#tag_13_49), which is included already and the compile flag `_XOPEN_SOURCE` was set to 700, but according to [POSIX 2004](http://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/) and [POSIX 1995](http://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/007908799/) it is only defined in `sys/types.h`. Including that fixed the compile error.

If undefined, I further set `_XOPEN_SOURCE 500`, just in case.

title: Make sure path is in native encoding
description:
Fixes #476 CP1251 char set in file name

Fixes #370 read_excel on Windows fails to open a file from a UTF-8 encoded path containing special characters

This is a new problem seen with R 3.5, we believe as a result of measures taken in response to [Bug 17120 ](https://bugs.r-project.org/bugzilla3/show_bug.cgi?id=17120):

In a non-UTF-8 locale (basically Windows?), `path.expand()` returns a UTF-8 encoded path, even for non UTF-8 input. readxl pre-processes xls paths via `normalizePath()`, which calls `path.expand()`. And then libxls uses `fopen()`, which expects the path in the native encoding.

We have two choices:

  1. Stop using `normalizePath()` on xls files. It's not clear to me why we do this. This code goes back to Day 3 of readxl development, in 2015 fc076c463dca90407e03a8c988df6c65936051bb. The history doesn't indicate if there is a reason to use `normalizePath()`. I explored "stop calling `normalizePath()`" in 945178d41dbef4b02a0ce56c7fffc1793d2eaed6, which passes tests. If we choose this, I will obviously remove more even code vs. comment it out.
  2. Keep using `normalizePath()` on xls files, but process immediately with `enc2native()`.  Explored in 8a8c06136c9254b029368c24dc34915f49af6d0c, which also passes tests.

Either way, I think we should consider incorporating the new test. However I decided `skip_on_cran()` might be wise.

title: Parse _rels/.rels to get paths to package parts
description:
Fixes #435 Be able to read sheets produced by the Los Angeles Police Department

The xlsx produced by LAPD is a very literal implementation of the example on pp65-66 of 5th edition of ECMA:

> Example: The following package represents the minimal conformant SpreadsheetML package as defined by ECMA-376

I used this as motivation to make a major upgrade to how readxl parses the package structure. Basically, readxl previously did not parse it but, rather, assumed a very common default. And the LAPD sheets show that other structures are possible (Excel can open the LAPD files, btw). Now we can read LAPD sheets, while still being able to read all the other weird 3rd party sheets in our test collection 🤞

The main feature of the LAPD sheets is that they do not use an `xl/` subdirectory, whereas every other xlsx we've seen before does. Browsable examples:

  * LAPD sheets do not use an `xl/` subdirectory: [excelgesis/los-angeles-arrests-xlsx](https://jennybc.github.io/excelgesis/los-angeles-arrests-xlsx/index.html)
  * [excelgesis/embedded-chartsheet](https://jennybc.github.io/excelgesis/embedded-chartsheet/index.html) is a good example of a "normal" xlsx with multiple worksheets and a chartsheet. It has an `xl/` subdirectory.
  * [excelgesis/Ekaterinburg_IP_9](https://jennybc.github.io/excelgesis/Ekaterinburg_IP_9/index.html) is a valuable example of yet another type of 3rd party xlsx. It uses `xl/` but insists on giving paths in `/xl/foo/bar` form in all the relationship files, which is peculiar (very different from embedded-chartsheet example). It's also completely in Cyrillic, which is extra fun.

title: Duplicating values for all previously merged cells, for .xlsx formats
description:
Currently, when merged cells in the `.xlsx` format become an R object, all individual cells that made up the merged cell are assigned `NA`, except for the top-left-most cell, which retains the original value. Something like the following:
Column1 Column2 Column3
OneAndTwo Three
One Two
becomes:
Column1 Column2 Column3
OneAndTwo NA Three
One Two NA
I believe that should not be thought of as the appropriate behavior--almost all information about where the merged cells were is lost, and at the very least, it seems less intuitive and aesthetically pleasing. To me, the preferred behavior should result in:
Column1 Column2 Column3
OneAndTwo OneAndTwo Three
One Two Three
In this pull request, I've added code that results that behavior for `.xlsx` files. In order to keep as much of the original code unaltered as possible, the function I added automatically duplicates the attributes and values of the node with the original value for the merged cell, and clones it into the empty cells that were once a part of the same merged cell, keeping their original references or whatever they're called (e.g. "B3", "F9", etc.). If people think it would be better to have this behavior be optional, I can add that in. Additionally, I can add tests if need be. Also, I was testing/editing the code on GitHub, so I have a _lot_ of commits. I don't know what people's philosophy is about that, but if it's preferable, I can go back and get rid of a lot of the annoying commits I made.

title: Account for leap year bug; fixes #264
description:
Excel reproduces a bug from Lotus 1-2-3: the non-existent leap day February 29, 1900 is included in the date system. This only affects sheets that use the 1900 date system and dates prior to March 1, 1900.

The proposed fix effectively removes that date. I adjust (increment) date-times on or before February 28, 1900. I convert date-times on February 29 1900 -- a day which does not actually exist -- to NA and throw a warning.

Since knowledge of the date system is now required for both the leap year adjustment and the offset, I store and pass the 1900 vs 1904 indicator around instead of the offset.

Fixes #264 and #148 (already closed as duplicate), if you want to read more about it.

In #309, we have an xls BIFF5, a very old format (but with recent data, so apparently some tool is still writing this!). It uses the LABEL record type to hold strings, which is an ancient practice and, I thought, no longer occurring. I was wrong.

title: LABEL records in xls 1) exist and 2) have length stored as 16-bit value; fix…
description:
…es #309 

Here is an alternative to #310 that is much more surgical and preserves my hard-earned clean report from memcheck!

### Restating the context

In #309, we have an xls BIFF5, a very old format (but with recent data, so apparently some tool is still writing this!). It uses the LABEL record type to hold strings, which is an ancient practice and, I thought, no longer occurring. I was wrong.

Problem 1: readxl had stopped reading LABEL cells. Hadley had covered this cell type, but I'd let it go missing in one place in my revisions. I've added it back and such cells are now loaded again.

Problem 2: The fix re: using longer integers to index into the shared string table (https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/pull/293) actually breaks the string extraction for LABEL records. All of this is libxls problems/bugs btw. The problem is that `label` needs to be a pointer to `uint32_t` for parsing modern BIFF8 sheets / LABELSST records and a pointer to `uint16_t` for sheets like the one in #309. This only matters for advancing `label` past the string length, so it points at the beginning of the string.

This solution just moves `label` backwards one byte inside `if(pWB->is5ver) {...}` to correct for the fact that `label++;` goes too far.

https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/0587f00dcc889bc263b232da4c1951c631b975f3/src/libxls/xlsstruct.h#L240-L246

https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/0587f00dcc889bc263b232da4c1951c631b975f3/src/xls.c#L152

But then it was indexing into the table with a 16 bit integer and therefore vulnerable to getting the wrong strings. It takes a large sheet to expose this, i.e. more than 65535 unique strings. Which is the case with the xls from #129.

Two questions:

  * Should I add a test for this? It would require a very large xls, plus it doesn't really seem like something readxl should be responsible for.
  * Should I try to push this change back into libxls? It's not trivial for me, because it's on sourceforge and uses svn, whereas I've only done this with Git/GitHub. Yet it's a tiny change and seems like a no-brainer.

title: Date subsecond rounding; fixes #187
description:
I know this is sort of horrible. But it's low tech and seems to work. The test sheets currently contain two cells: the problematic date-time from #187 and another from the analogous issue thread from the SheetJS world. Before this fix, the test fails and after it passes. My intention is to produce a date-time in R that matches the one in Excel to at least the second. I recommend you stop reading here.

*Notes after excessive amounts of study*: You might think this problem only depends on time of day, since Excel's serial dates use a natural unit of 1, with the decimal part capturing the time of day. And you might then create a comprehensive test sheet with one row per second in a day and use various ways to test that you import this sheet correctly, at least to 1 second accuracy. But you would be wrong.

The floating point number recorded by Excel for a specific time of day depends, in completely mysterious ways, on both the day and whether the date-time is hard-coded ("typed") vs. formula vs. "paste by value" from a formula. For example, the problematic date-times mentioned above are NOT problematic in the context of a sheet that holds one row per second in the day or for other days in history.

Here are the numbers recorded in `xl/worksheets/sheet???.xml` for a cell holding 11:30am in various scenarios:

  * Hand-typed for 2016-04-28: 42488.479166666664
  * Computed via formula, by adding 1 second repeatedly to a base of 00:00:00 on 2016-04-28: 42488.479166778678
  * Hand-typed, same time of day, but on 2017-01-01: 42736.479166666664
  * Hand-typed, same time of day, but on 1954-01-01: 19725.479166666668

I think you can only trust Excel's floating point representation of a date-time to the n-th decimal place. You should go part way there, round, send that info to R, and be thankful you got this far.

Another exercise that yielded super-weird results: I write one date-time for each second in a specific day. Import that into Excel and write to xlsx. Import that xlsx into R and take the sequential differences via `diff.POSIXt()`. They should all be 1. But they are not. And the actual values, cardinality, etc. vary in impenetrable ways, depending on which day in history you examine.

title: Create data member for cell type; align XlsWorkBook/XlsWorkSheet w/ xlsx counterparts
description:

As discussed, I reworked XlsWorkBook and XlsWorkSheet to have an interface like the xlsx counterparts. Now an XlsWorkBook object only holds data, no longer points to an open workbook, and can "belong" to an XlsWorkSheet object. Therefore an XlsWorkSheet does have to (re-)open the workbook and then the requested sheet. But this cleared the way for `read_xls_()` and `read_xlsx_()` to be identical.

Main points:

  * Checking whether cell contents match the values in the `na` argument is now generally delegated to the `type()` member function of both XlsCell and XlsxCell. If the reported type is not CELL_BLANK, then the cell has contents you should work with. I have not exploited this to the maximum extent possible yet tbh, but am working on it.

title: Patch xls.c to read all cols in xls written by some third-party s/w; …
description:
…fixes #152, fixes #99 

Sheets report their dimension and libxls exposes that as `lastrow` and `lastcol`. xls written by Excel tends to report `lastrow` as the 0-indexed maximum row but reports `lastcol` as the 1-indexed maximum col (or reports the total number of columns). So an `n` by `p` sheet would have `lastrow = n - 1` and `lastcol = p`. I assume that's the origin of [this comment](https://github.com/tidyverse/readxl/blob/6c76a9b771c7b4b9c3e4c8f2036e4f0e78517f85/src/XlsWorkSheet.h#L32).

libxls seems to have baked this peculiarity into its cell reading logic.

But some 3rd party s/w writes xls that declares its dimension in the same manner for row and column. In which case libxls and, therefore, readxl fail to read the last column.

There's no way to fix it in readxl. This little change to `xls.c` fixes it.

title: Add `col_type = "list"` option
description:
This PR adds the ability to read in a column as a list of length-1 vectors, preserving the type given to the cell by excel.

I can imagine a lot of ways to solve this class of problems, but I found it useful when working with an excel worksheet where a bunch of cells were supposed to be of the form "NUMBER-NUMBER" but were converted to dates by excel. 

I also think there should be a warning when readxl encounters excel dates in text or numeric columns. I find it confusing that it silently gives a number, even if the original date is technically recoverable from the number. I'm happy to add that here, or in a separate PR if you prefer.

```r
library(readxl)
library(purrr)
library(lubridate)
library(dplyr)

example <- read_excel("example.xls")

example
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>           var1
#>          <chr>
#> 1        30-30
#> 2        20-20
#> 3 43018.000000

example <- read_excel("example.xls", col_type = "list") %>%
  mutate(var1 = map_if(var1, is.POSIXct, ~paste0(month(.), "-", day(.))) %>% flatten_chr)

example
#> # A tibble: 3 × 1
#>    var1
#>   <chr>
#> 1 30-30
#> 2 20-20
#> 3 10-10
```

title: Refactor xlsx col type handling
description:
1. If user wants to skip a column, now we say `"skip"` instead of `"blank"`. Created a new `CellType`, `CELL_SKIP` for this. Existing `CellType`, `CELL_BLANK` now really means what it says.

    We're using `CellType` for 2 different concepts that almost coincide but not quite: cell type and column type. I thought about separating them but it didn't seem worth it. A very recent PR (#256) from a user proposes to implement a `"list"` type, where each cell can have the type declared in the Excel. And he, possibly out of necessity, had to separate the cell type from column type. Something to think about.

1. Leading and embedded empty columns are never dropped.

1. If `col_types` has length one, recycle it to have length = number of columns.

1. More effort to make sense of user-specified `col_names`, if there are also user-specified `col_types`. Specifically, if column(s) will be skipped, accept full-length `col_names` or `col_names` post-skip. *I suspect you might not approve of this?*

AWKWARD: a few things had to be fixed or improved. But it doesn't seem to make sense to build up a flexible col spec system in readxl, since it should just work like readr (#198). But that would require pulling lots of logic out of readr into a col spec package. Which isn't imminent. 🤔

title: Don't load empty cells; use empirical worksheet dimensions
description:
There can be cells that look empty to the human eye, but that are styled, e.g. someone applied a custom number format to the cell at some point. I propose we do not load those anymore. There's nothing to learn from their XML.

If such a cell still falls into the target rectangle, it will simply be `NA` in the output (ok, won't be totally true until we stop dropping unnamed, empty columns #157).

If such a cell falls outside the target rectangle, this PR prevents the creation of trailing row(s) or column(s) consisting entirely of `NA`.

In addition to rows/columns of `NA`, this has been a puzzling source of errors about column names and types not being compatible.

To fully fix this, you also can't trust a worksheet's declared dimensions, because these cells "count". Therefore I propose we always compute dimension ourselves.

I haven't dealt with xls yet. I can leave this open and work on that. Or we could resolve this for xlsx and I'd open an issue to fix it for xls.

This branch builds off #247. I'm assuming it will be merged first.

title: Fix for .xlsx containing 'unicode character expressions' such as _x000D_.
description:
This closes out #51.  It appears Excel (assuming that's what produced the spreadsheet the provided) doesn't obey it's own advice, as 0xD is perfectly valid in XML v1.0.  In any case, this occurs, so should be supported.

As far as I could tell (with an admittedly brief look) the regex stuff in R is not available on the C side, and as this was an easy thing to look for at any rate, the iterative code isn't too bad given we stay in C-land.

Note the use of the GraphicsDevice.h function (clearly someone else needed to do this at some point!) which at this stage is just exported directly until the code is finalised, but should really be pulled in via the include, which has the same definition.  Using Riconv directly is ugly, thus the existence of this function!

Another alternate would be to include the 15 lines or so required to convert unicode (i.e. utf32) codepoints to utf8 which is easy enough (and would be faster as no need to construct the Riconv object or perform the buffer manipulation).

Finally, another alternate would be to jump to R land and do something like `eval(parse("'\\u000D'"))` after first constructing that string via gsub to get R to parse each chunk directly. (Speed probably isn't an issue here).
